Meeting Schedule

The regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month,
closed session business will usually commence at 5:30 p.m., when scheduled, and general business
session will commence at 6:30 p.m.

Brown Act

Agendas are drafted to accurately state what the legislative body is being asked to consider. The
legislative body can take action on "all items" listed on the agenda and be in compliance with the open
meeting laws. Under the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the
agenda, or unless certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The governing body may direct
staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for consideration at a future meeting.

City's Vision Statement

We envision a thriving, safe and inclusive community where everyone has the opportunity to access
exceptional services, education and support to be resilient and live full, vibrant lives.

Public Communications

Public Comments on agenda items are limited to three (3) minutes. All comments are to be addressed
directly to the Agency Members not to the members of the public.

Emails for public comment received prior to 4:00 pm on the day of the Council Meeting will be
summarized by the City Clerk, not read in its entirety. A copy of the email will be provided to the City
Council and will also be available at the City Clerk's Office for public review. A copy of each email will be
recorded for public record and noted on the official minutes of tonight's meeting.

GENERAL NOTICE TO THE PUBLIC

The City Council adopted new rules relating to the conduct of the public meetings, proceedings, and
business in the City of South Gate on July 12, 2022, (Resolution 2022-38-CC) and go into effect on
August 1, 2022. Resolution #2022-38-CC is available at the City Clerk’s Office.

MEETING SCHEDULE

Regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month, closed
session meetings will commence at 5:30 p.m. unless posted otherwise on its agenda. The regular City
Council meetings will commence at 6:30 p.m. Agendas are available at the following locations: City Clerk
Office, Public Notice Boards at City Hall, and on the City’s web page at https://www.cityofsouthgate.org

The Public can sign up to receive automatic notices of postings of agendas for the City Council or any
other Commission or Board of the City of South Gate. Visit the City webpage and click on the Agenda &
Minutes icon. That will take you the page where an individual can enter their email in the “Email
Updates” box to register.

PUBLIC COMMENT/PARTICIPATION

Any person may request to address a legislative body during a public meeting. The Presiding Officer will
call upon those present in the Council Chambers.

Speakers are limited to three (3) minutes on any item listed on the agenda, including public hearings.
Under Comments from the Audience portion, speakers are also limited to a single three (3) minutes time
limit. Comments from the Audience is initially limited to 45 minutes at each meeting. Any speaker still
wishing to speak, that did not speak, will have an addition Comments from the Audience opportunity after
the last business item is finished. The Presiding Officer may extend the time limit as long as there is no
objection from the City Council as a body.

To ensure that the public is able to participate, the City provides the opportunity to submit their
comments in person, email, mail. Methods of participation may be subject to change during other such

  8
 times when a State of Emergency, Health Order or State Executive Order limits in-person participation.

CURFEW

In absence of a motion duly adopted by majority vote of the City Council, the Presiding Officer may
adjourn the City Council meetings at 10:30 p.m. The Presiding Officer may ask the City Council if any
agenda items listed should be continued or dealt with during the meeting. For those items to be
continued, the City Council can direct the item be placed on the next City Council agenda or the current
meeting may be adjourned to a time certain at which time the meeting shall be reconvened as an
Adjourned Regular Meeting of the City Council and action upon the published agenda continued.

STAFF REPORTS

As a general rule, staff reports. or other written documentation are prepared/organized with respect to
each item of business listed on the agenda. Meeting agendas and staff reports are available at least 72-
hours prior to the scheduled regular City Council meeting and a minimum of 24-hours prior to a Special
City Council meeting. There are times when the City Council receives written material. revised material
after the posting of agendas, these materials are become a public record and will be available for public
view within 72-hours after the meeting in which they were received. Those materials and any other public
document can be inspected in the City Clerk's Office located at 8650 California Avenue, South Gate.

SERVICES TO FACILITATE ACCESS TO PUBLIC MEETINGS

In compliance with the American with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in the
City Council Meetings, please contact the Office of the City Clerk. Notification 48 hours prior to the City
Council Meeting will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to assure accessibility. For
further information, please contact the Office of the City Clerk at (323) 563-9510 or via email at
yglaze@sogate.org.

  PURPOSE:  To ask the City Council  to introduce,  by firstreading,  an Ordinance  comprehensively
  amending  Chapter 1.54 ofthe  South Gate Municipal  Code (Purchasing  System andBidding  Rules)
  and to set second reading  and adoption  for theregularmeeting  of September  22, 2026. The current

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  Adoption  ofthis  Ordinance  requires  afour-fifthsvote  ofthe  City
  Council,  because Section  1,54.370(B)  of the amended  Chapter  delegates  emergency  contracting
  authority  to the City Manager  and Public  Contract  Code Section  22050(b)(1)  requires  that such a
  delegation  be made by a four-fifths  vote. The City  Council  will  consider:

  a.  Introducing  the proposed  Ordinance  amending  Chapter  1.54 of the South Gate Municipal
  Code by reading  title only and waiving  further  reading;  and

  b.  Setting the second reading  and adoption  of the Ordinance  for the regular  meeting  of
  September 22, 2026.

  S[TMMARY:  Chapter 1.54 governshowthe  City buys goods, contracts  for setvices,  awards public
  works  projects,  and disposes  of surplus  property.  The current  Chapter  was last comprehensively
  updated in 2005 and shows its age in four respects.

  First, several provisions  no longertrack  current  state and federal law. The current  Chapterrequires
  payment  bonds  on public  works  contracts  only  above  $100,000,  while  California  Civil  Code
  Section  9550 mandates  paytnent  bonds  on all  California  local  public  works  contracts  above
  $25,000.  The current  Chapter  does not address  the Public  Contract  Code  Section  22050(c)(2)

  1

  10
 timing  for Council  review  and ratification  of emergency  procurements.  The current  Chapter  cites
Article  XI  Section  8 of the California  Constitution  for intergovernmental  contracts,  where  the
controlling  authority  is the Joint Exercise  of Powers  Act at Governrnent  Code Section  6500 et seq.

Second,  dollar  thresholds  set in 2005 are now,  in some cases, too low to reflect  current  operational
reality  and, in other  cases, create uru'iecessary  Council  touches  on routine  transactions.  The open
market  threshold  of $2,000 has not been adjusted  in over 20 years,  creating  a paperwork  burden
for routine purchases. The administrative  disposition  limit  for surplus  property  of $1,000  sends
low-value  items to the Council  for individual  approval.

Third,  the  current  Chapter  is silent  on procurement  methods  that  have  become  standard  in

California  municipal  practice,  including  design-build  and progressive  design-build  delivery  for
public  works  (authorized  under Public  Contract  Code Section  22160  et seq. and Section  22170  et
seq. respectively,  for the categories  of agency  and project  those chapters  cover),  on-call  and master
service  agreements  with task-order  structures,  cooperative  and piggyback  purchasing  under proper
certification,  and e-procurement  portal-based  notice  and award.

Fourth,  the  current  Chapter  does  not  address  how  procurement  procedures  change  during  a
proclaimed  local,  state,  or federal  emergency.  South  Gate's  experience  during  the COVID-19
response,  the 2020 windstorm,  and other  recent  emergencies  confirmed  that  the City  needs  a
codified  emergency  procurement  framework  with  clear delegation  tiers,  ratification  procedures,
and operational  mechanisms.

The proposed  Ordinance  addresses  all four  concerns.  It brings  the four  critical  legal  compliance
provisions  into alignment  with  the current  statute.  It rationalizes  dollar  thresholds  where  the 2005
figures  have  become  operationally  burdensome,  while  preserving  the existing  $50,000  formal
bidding  threshold.  It introduces  modern  procurement  methods  that California  municipal  practice
has adopted.  It establishes  a comprehensive  emergency  procurement  framework.  And  it adds new
internal-control  provisions,  including  an anti-splitting  prohibition  (Section  1.54.165),  a funding
eligibility  certification  at the department  level  (Section  1.54.140(B)),  and an annual  inflation
adjustment  mechanism  subject  to Council  resolution  (Section  1.54.030(B)).

The proposed  Ordinance  has undergone  extensive  legal  review  by the City  Attorney's  Office,
including  a final  review  by outside  counsel  retained  by the City  Attorney.  All  material  legal
compliance  items have been addressed,  and the City  Attorney's  Office  concurs  with  first reading.

FISCAL  IMPACT:  Adoption  of the proposed  Ordinance  has no direct  fiscal  impact  on the fiscal
year 2026-27  General  Fund or any other fund.  The Ordinance  changes  how the City  procures,  not
whether  it procures.  Ongoing  operational  efficiencies  are expected  from  reduced  paperwork
burden on routine  purchases  and faster  processing  of administrative-tier  transactions,  but these
efficiencies  are not quantifiable  in advance  with  sufficient  confidence  to book  as savings.

Two  indirect  fiscal  implications  are worth  noting.  First,  aligning  the payment  bond threshold  with
Civil  Code  Section  9550,  which  currently  requires  a payment  bond  on public  works  contracts  in
excess of $25,000  rather  than the $100,000  threshold  in the current  Chapter,  brings  the City  into
compliance  and reduces  exposure  on small public  works  contracts  by giving  unpaid  subcontractors
and suppliers  recourse  against  the bond,  which  is the remedy  the Civil  Code contemplates,  rather
than leaving  the City  to manage  stop payment  notices  and withheld  funds.  Second,  the 'funding

  2
  11
 eligibility  certification  at Section  1.54.140(B)  is designed  to protect  the  General  Fund  from
inadvertent  commingling  of restricted  'funds by placing  primary  responsibility  for funding-source
compliance  on the requesting  department  rather  than Finance  staff verification  at the requisition
stage. This  is an internal  control  improvement  that may reduce  the risk of external  Single  Audit
findings  in :[uture years.

ANALYSIS:  The proposed  Ordinance  is organized  into  the same subject  areas as the current
Chapter,  but  the  substantive  content  has been  comprehensively  rewritten.  The  Change  Map
(Attachment  3) walks  through  the principal  substantive  differences  between  the current  Chapter
and  the  proposed  Ordinance,  organized  by  topic.  The  following  sections  describe  the  four
functional  areas of the rewrite  at a level  appropriate  for Council  consideration.

Modernization  and Competition

The proposed  Ordinance  retains  the existing  $50,000  formal  bidding  threshold,  which  Council  has
held  at this  level  since  2005.  Below  that  threshold,  the  Ordinance  restructures  the  informal
procurement  framework.  The  open-market  threshold  (where  documented  price  reasonableness,
rather  than  three  written  quotes,  is sufficient)  increases  from  $2,000  to $3,000.  The  internal
approval  band for the Director  of Administrative  Services  to sign off on an award  (in addition  to
the  department  manager  requisition)  increases  from  $5,000  to $25,000.  The  $50,000  formal
bidding  threshold,  above which  Council  award is required,  is unchanged.  Raising  the internal  band
does mean that purchases  between  $5,000  and $25,000  no longer  require  Director-level  sign-off
before  award,  which  is a real change  in internal  routing  rather  than a change  in the level  at which
Council  acts.

The Ordinance  also adds an anti-splitting  prohibition  at Section  1.54.165,  which  is standard  in
California  municipal  procurement  codes  adopted  in the last decade.  The prohibition  aggregates
substantially  similar  fiscal-year  needs  for  threshold  determination  purposes,  while  permitting
unbundling  where  doing  so would  expand  small  business,  minority  business  enterprise,  women's
business  enterprise,  labor  surplus  area  firm,  or  qualified  South  Gate  business  participation,
consistent  with  2 CFR Section  200.321(b)(3).

Notice  and award  procedures  shift from  newspaper  publication  as the primary  method  to the City's
e-procurement  portal.  Newspaper  notice  is retained  where  required  by law (Public  Contract  Code
Section  22037  publication  for formal  public  works  bidding,  for example)  or where  the Purchasing
Officer  determines  newspaper  publication  is advantageous  to the City.  This  change  reflects  how
vendors  actually  find  solicitations  in 2026 and reduces  the cost of solicitation  advertising.

Public  Works  and CIP  Deliveiy

The Ordinance  retains  the City's  existing  election  to be subject  to the Uniform  Public  Construction
Cost  Accounting  Act  (UPCCAA)  at Public  Contract  Code  Section  22000  et seq. Rather  than
restating  the  UPCCAA  dollar  figures,  the proposed  Ordinance  refers  to the  state  thresholds
directly,  so the  Chapter  follows  future  state  adjustments  without  further  Council  action.  The
thresholds  currently  in effect  under  Public  Contract  Code  Section  22032,  as amended  effective
January 1, 2025, are force account or negotiated  contract  up to $75,000,  informal  bidding  up to
$220,000, and formal bidding above $220,000.

 The Ordinance  also adds, for the first time in South  Gate's Municipal  Code,  authority  for design-
build  and progressive  design-build  delivery  on public  works  projects  (Section  1.54.467),  authority
for the Public  Works  Director  to pre-qualify  bidders  on larger  projects  (Section  1.54.430(C)),  and
a maintenance  contract  framework  for work  that is not a public  project  under Public  Contract  Code
Section  22002  (Section  1.54.486).  All  three are authorized  under  California  statute.  Design-build
and progressive  design-build  are available  only for the categories  of project  the enabling  chapters
cover,  are subject  to statutory  cost  floors,  project-count  limits,  workforce  requirements,  and
reporting  duties,  and are subject  to statutory  expiration  dates. There  are two  separate  progressive
design-build  pathways.  Public  Contract  Code Section  22170  et seq. reaches  water  and wastewater
projects  and expires  January  1, 2029. Public  Contract  Code Section  22185  et seq., added by Senate
Bill  706 in 2023, reaches public  works  generally,  is capped  at ten projects  in excess of $5,000,000
each, carries  a skilled  and trained  workforce  requirement,  and expires  January  1, 2030.  Section
1.54.467  authorizes  both  pathways  and leaves  the  choice  between  them  to the  project-level
eligibility  determination.  Section  1.54.467  therefore  authorizes  these methods  only  for projects
that are eligible  under  state law,  requires  written  confirmation  of eligibility  in consultation  with
the City  Attorney  before  a solicitation  is issued,  and leaves  the current  eligibility  criteria  and
thresholds  to the Administrative  Purchasing  Policies  and Procedures  so they  can be updated  as
state law  changes.  Adding  the authority  to the Municipal  Code  does not  by  itself  make  any
particular  City  project  eligible.

Internal  Controls  and Compliance

The Ordinance  addresses  the four critical  legal compliance  items identified  earlier:  the Civil  Code
Section  9550  payment  bond  threshold  (now  $25,000,  matching  state law);  the Public  Contract
Code  Section  22050(c)(2)  emergency  review  and ratification  timing  (now  explicitly  tracked  in
Section  1.54.370(B)(2));  the Labor  Code  Section  1771  prevailing  wage  requirement  for public
works  above  $1,000  and the  Labor  Code  Section  1771.1  contractor  and subcontractor  DIR
registration  requirements  (Section  1.54.495);  and the Government  Code  Section  6500  et seq.
citation  for intergovernmental  contracts  (Section  1.54.510(I)).

The Ordinance  also addresses  federal  grant compliance  comprehensively  at Section  1.54.050(B),
which  incorporates  2 CFR  Sections  200.317  through  200.327  by reference  and addresses  Davis-
Bacon  prevailing  wage on federally  funded  construction  prime  contracts  above  $2,000  where  the
federal  program  legislation  or  award  terms  impose  it,  the  socioeconomic  affirmative  steps
encouraged  by 2 CFR  Section  200.321  for  small,  minority,  women,  veteran-owned,  and labor
surplus  area businesses,  conflict  of interest  standards,  and full and open competition  requirements.
Consistent  with  the 2024 revisions  to the Uniform  Guidance,  those steps are stated in the Chapter
as encouraged  rather  than required,  so that the City  is not held to a standard  more restrictive  than
federal  law  imposes.  The  funding  eligibility  certification  at  Section  1.54.140(B)  places
responsibility  for confirming  funding-source  eligibility  on the requesting  department,  the project
manager,  and  the  department  head,  with  Finance  verifying  the  available  appropriation.  This
division  of responsibility  better  matches  actual  program  knowledge  to the certification  function
and protects  Finance's  internal  controls  during  Single  Audit  and grantor  monitoring.

Bond  and insurance  requirements  at Section  1.54.490  conform  to state law.  Payment  bonds  are
mandatory  at 100%  of the contract  amount  for public  works  contracts  exceeding  the threshold  set
by Civil  Code  Section  9550,  which  is currently  $25,000.  The  Ordinance  refers  to the statutory
threshold  rather  than restating  the figure,  so the requirement  tracks  any future  change  in state law.

City  policy  choice  unchanged  from  the current  Chapter)  and discretionary  for contracts  below  that

Emergency  Procurement  Framework

The  Ordinance  establishes  a comprehensive  emergency  procurement  framework  at Section
1.54.370  for  use  during  a proclaimed  local,  state,  or  federal  emergency.  Under  Section
1.54.370(B),  the City  Council  delegates  the Public  Contract  Code  Section  22050  emergency
contracting  authority  to the City  Manager,  which  state law  permits  only  by a four-fi:[ths  vote.
Section  1.54.370(C)  does not itself  delegate  statutory  authority.  It sets the internal  routing  by which
the City Manager's  delegated  authority  is exercised  within  the organization:  a Department  Director
may  approve  up to $25,000  per procurement,  the Director  of Administrative  Services  up to
$100,000,  and the City  Manager  up to $500,000, with  matters  above  $500,000 going to the City
Council  except  where  the City  Manager  makes  a written  determination  that the emergency  does
not permit  delay  for Council  action.  The City  Manager  remains  accountable  to the Council  for all
action  taken  under  the delegation.  The  delegated  officer  reports  the reasons  for  the action  as
required  by Public  Contract  Code Section  22050(b)(3),  and the City  Council  conducts  the initial
and  continuing  review  required  by  Section  22050(c)(2).  Section  1.54.370(B)(5)  states  that
emergency  purchases  outside  the scope  of Section  22050,  such  as sheltering,  mass  care,  and
continuity  of operations,  rest on the City's  general  purchasing  authority  rather  than  on Section
22050,  and are reported  to Council  on the same schedule.

The  framework  also  authorizes  operational  mechanisms  during  emergencies  (Section
1.54.370(D)):  elevated  P-card  limits,  advance  payments  to vendors,  pre-screened  cooperative
purchasing  with  abbreviated  certification  (full  certification  within  30 days),  after-hours  and
electronic-signature  execution,  and  other  necessary  operational  mechanisms  the  Director  of
Administrative  Services  determines  consistent  with  applicable  law  and  funding-source
requirements.  These  mechanisms  reflect  lessons  learned  from  the  City's  response  during  the
COVID-19  emergency  and other declared  emergencies.

Changes  in Delegated  Authority

The  Ordinance  expands  administrative  authority  in six respects.  The City  Manager  may  award
professional  services  contracts  up to $100,000,  where  the  current  Chapter  leaves  professional
services  award  authority  to a separate  administrative  instruction  (Section  1.54.350(D)(1)).  Task
orders  up to $250,000 may be issued  administratively  against  a Council-approved  master  service
agreement,  within  the aggregate  cap the Council  approved  at award  (Section  1.54.355(D)(2)).  The
Public  Works  Director  may approve  change  orders  up to the lesser of 10 percent  of the original
contract  amount  or $250,000  cumulatively,  where  the current  Chapter  uses a 20 percent  test with
a $50,000  or $100,000  ceiling  (Section  1.54.610(B)).  The Director  of Administrative  Services  may
approve  modifications  to informally  awarded  supply  and service  contracts  on a comparable  basis
(Section  1.54.610(C)).  The administrative  limit  for disposing  of surplus  property  rises from  $1,000
to $10,000  (Section  1.54.810(C)).  The  Public  Works  Director  may  award  informal  UPCCAA
public  works  contracts  up to the state informal  bidding  threshold,  currently  $220,000,  which  Public
Contract  Code  Section  22034(c)  expressly  permits  a governing  body  to  delegate  (Section
1 .54.450(C)).

 Legal  Review

The City  Attorney's  Office  reviewed  the proposed  Ordinance  over the past year of drafting,  and
all  legal  compliance  items  identified  during  that  review  were  incorporated  into  the  version
transmitted  with  this report.  The City  Attorney's  Office  concurs  with  first reading.

CEQA  Determination

The proposed  Ordinance  is not a project  under the California  Environmental  Quality  Act (CEQA)
because it consists  of administrative  and procedural  changes to the City's  purchasing  code and does
not have  the potential  to result  in either  a direct  physical  change  or a reasonably  foreseeable
indirect  physical  change  in the environment  (CEQA  Guidelines  Section  15378(b)(2)  and (b)(5)).
To the extent  the Ordinance  authorizes  specific  future  public  works  projects  (for  example,  by
adding  design-build  authority),  each such future  project  will  be subject  to its own  CEQA  review
at the time  it is considered  for approval.

Implementation  and Effective  Date

The Ordinance  becomes  effective  30 days after  second  reading  and adoption  on September  22,
2026,  with  an effective  date of October  22, 2026.  Section  6 of the Ordinance  sets a separate
operative  date of December  21, 2026, three months  after adoption.  Chapter  1.54, as it reads today,
continues  to govern  procurement  until  the operative  date. The purpose  of the delay  is to give the
City  time  to issue the implementing  Administrative  Purchasing  Policies  and Procedures  (APPP)
and to complete  department  training  before  the new rules  apply,  rather  than putting  departments
under  a new  Chapter  that  has not yet been trained.  The  amended  Chapter,  therefore,  becomes
operative  during  the second  quarter  of fiscal  year 2026-27,  leaving  roughly  seven months  under
the new Chapter  before  the close of the fiscal  year.

Stafftraining  on the new Chapter  is planned,  covering  the new approval  authorities  and the funding
eligibility  certification  process,  as well  as department-analyst  training  on operational  procedures
and forms.  Both training  waves are scheduled  to conclude  before  December  21, 2026, the operative
date, and the APPP  will  be issued  in advance  of the first training  wave.

Procedural  Considerations

This  Ordinance  is brought  to Council  for first  reading  on September  8, 2026,  and second  reading
and adoption  on September  22, 2026.  Government  Code Section  36934  provides  that an ordinance
may not be passed within  five days of its introduction,  and not at other than a regular  or adjourned
regular  meeting.  It also provides  that an ordinance  must be read in full  at introduction  or passage
unless  further  reading  is waived  by regular  motion  adopted  by majority  vote,  or unless  the title
appears  on the published  agenda  and the full  text is available  to the public  online  and in print  at
the meeting.  The fourteen  days between  the two meetings  satisfies  the five-day  requirement.  If the
Ordinance  is altered  after introduction,  Section  36934  requires  that it be passed at a meeting  held
at least  five  days  after  the  alteration;  corrections  of typographical  or clerical  errors  are not
alterations  for this  purpose.  Following  adoption,  the City  Clerk  will  publish  the Ordinance  as
required  by Government  Code Section  36933.  Because  the amended  Chapter  is lengthy,  the City
Clerk  intends  to publish  a summary  under  Section  36933(c)(1)  and to post a certified  copy of the
full  text  in the Clerk's  office  not less than  five  days before  the September  22, 2026,  adoption

1.54.010  Purpose  and  organization  of this  chapter.

This Chapter establishes  the rules under which the City of South Gate purchases  supplies,
equipment,  and services; the competitive  bidding procedures  that apply to those purchases;  and
a separate  bidding system for public projects and maintenance  work. It also sets the standards
of conduct that apply to every City procurement,  authorizes a local business credit, governs
contract modifications  and change  orders, adopts  an environmentally  preferable  purchasing
policy, and establishes  procedures  for disposition  of surplus City property.

1.54.030  Changes  to dollar  limits.

A. State-Law  Threshold  Updates. State-law  dollar thresholds  expressly  incorporated  by
reference  in this Chapter (including  those in the uniform  Public Construction  Cost Accounting
Act and elsewhere)  shall be applied as amended  from time to time, without further Council
action.

B. Annual Inflation Adjustment.  As part of the annual budget process, the Director of
Administrative  Services shall calculate an inflation adjustment  equal to the percentage  change
in the GDP Implicit Price Deflator for State and Local Government  Consumption  Expenditures
(BEA NIPA Table 1.1.9) for the four quarters ending December  31 of the prior calendar year, not
less than zero percent (0%) and not more than three percent (3%), and shall present it to the
City Council. If the City Council adopts the adjustment  by resolution,  it applies to every dollar
amount stated in this Chapter,  rounded to the nearest one thousand  dollars ($1,000), except (1 )
the fifty thousand  dollar ($50,000)  formal bidding threshold in Sections 1.54.310,  1.54.320,  and
1.54.486,  which may be changed only by ordinance,  and (2) amounts set by state or federal
law, which are governed  by subsection  (A). Amounts  remain unchanged  in any year the City
Council does not adopt a resolution.  The Director of Administrative  Services shall publish the
amounts then in effect in the Administrative  Purchasing  Policies and Procedures.

1.54.055  Standards  of Conduct;  Conflicts  of Interest;  Gratuities.

This Section  supplements,  and does  not replace,  the conflict-of-interest  and ethics  requirements
imposed by Government  Code § 1090, the Political Reform Act (Government  Code §§ 81000  et
seq.), the regulations of the Fair Political Practices Commission, the common  law conflict-of-

  Page 7 of 29
  29
 interest doctrine, the City's conflict-of-interest code adopted under  the Political  Reform  Act, and
applicable  federal requirements  including 2 CFR § 200.318(c).

A. City elected  officials,  appointed  officials,  board  and commission  members,  officers,
employees,  and agents involved in the selection, award, or administration  of contracts  (including
federally funded contracts subject to 2 CFR § 200.31 8(c)) shall avoid any real or apparent
conflicts of interest. No person covered by this subsection  shall participate  in the selection,
award, or administration  of a contract supported  by City or federal funds if a real or apparent
conflict of interest would be involved. Such a conflict arises when an employee,  officer, official,
or board or commission  member, or any member of their immediate  family, has a financial or
other interest in, or receives a tangible personal benefit from, a firm considered  for a contract.
For purposes  of this Section, "immediate  family" means spouse or registered  domestic  partner,
parent, child, sibling, parent-in-law,  child-in-law,  or sibling-in-law, whether biological,  adoptive,
or by marriage.

B. City elected officials, appointed  officials, board and commission  members,  officers,
employees,  and agents shall not solicit or accept gratuities,  favors, or anything of monetary
value from present or prospective  contractors  or subcontractors  that could reasonably  be
perceived  to influence a procurement  decision.

C. Violations  of this Section are subject to disciplinary  action and may result in remedies  up to
and including  contract termination, disqualification,  or debarment  consistent with applicable  law.

D. Organizational  Conflicts  of Interest  (OCI).  A person  or firm that prepares  specifications,
statements  of work, or solicitation  documents  for a particular  procurement  shall not compete for
that procurement,  unless the City determines  in writing that adequate  safeguards  have been
implemented  to neutralize  or mitigate the conflict consistent  with applicable  law and funding-
source requirements.  The Administrative  Purchasing  Policies and Procedures  shall include the
standard  organizational  conflict-of-interest  guidelines  required of local agencies  using design-
build or progressive  design-build  delivery under Public Contract Code §§ 22160 et seq., 22170
et seq., and 22185 et seq.

E. Debarment  and Suspension.  The City may debar  or suspend  a vendor,  contractor,  or
consultant  for cause, including,  but not limited to, fraud, collusion,  a criminal offense in
connection  with obtaining  or performing  a public contract, significant  or repeated  performance
failures, or serious ethical violations.  The procedures,  notice, and appeal rights for debarment  or
suspension  shall be established  by administrative  policy consistent  with applicable  law.

All City contracts  shall include  non-discrimination  requirements  consistent  with Federal  and
State law and City policy, prohibiting  unlawful discrimination  in employment  and in performance
under the contract. The Purchasing  Officer shall include standard  contract  language to
implement  this section.

"1.54.057  Insurance,  Bonds,  and  Risk  Transfer.

A. Administrative  policy.  Minimum  insurance,  bonding,  indemnity,  and other  risk transfer
requirements  shall be established  by administrative  policy issued by the City Manager or
designee.  The policy may establish tiered requirements  based on the type of work, activity, or
exposure  presented,  and may be updated administratively  to reflect current standards, including
guidance  from the City's joint powers insurance  authority and its risk program advisors.

 B. Application.  The policy applies to any contract, purchase order, professional  services
agreement,  master service agreement,  task order, construction  contract, lease, license, permit,
facility use agreement,  special event authorization,  or other agreement  under which a person or
entity provides goods or services to the City, performs work on the City's behalf, or uses or
occupies  City property.  The policy  may provide  risk-based  exemptions  for low-risk  or de minimis
transactions.

C. Higher  requirements. A department  may require  limits or coverages  higher  than the policy
minimums  based on the risk presented.

D. Condition  precedent.  No agreement  subject to the policy shall be executed,  no notice to
proceed issued, and no work commenced  or goods or services delivered,  until the required
insurance,  endorsements,  bonds, and other security have been submitted  and verified as
provided by the policy.

E. Waiver. A reduction,  modification,  or waiver of a requirement  established by the policy is
effective only if approved  in writing by the City Manager, the Director of Administrative  Services,
or the City's Risk Manager,  and retained in the file. A Department  Director may not waive an
insurance  requirement.

F. Indemnity.  Indemnity and defense provisions shall be drafted  consistent with applicable law,
including Civil Code §§ 2782 and 2782.8, and with the standard  forms issued under the policy.

G. Bonds and other security. Bond requirements  for public works contracts  are governed  by
Section 1.54.490 and applicable state law. For all other agreements,  the Purchasing  Officer or
the Risk Manager may require bonds, letters of credit, or other security based on the risk
presented,  as provided  by the policy.

H. Administration.  The City may use a third-party  administrator to receive, review, and monitor
certificates  of insurance  and related documentation.  Use of an administrator  does not transfer
the City's approval or waiver authority.

1. Continuing  compliance.  Required coverage  shall be maintained  for the full term of the
agreement  and for any applicable completed  operations  or extended  reporting period. A lapse  is
a material breach, and the City may withhold  payment,  suspend work, or terminate.

1.54.710  Purpose  of environmentally  preferable  purchasing  policy.

The purpose of Sections 1.54.710  through 1.54.750  is to promote purchase of recycled  and
environmentally preferable  products,  minimize environmental  impacts of city operations,  and
support markets for recycled and sustainable  products.

1.54.720  Definitions  used  in environmentally  preferable  purchasing  policy.

A. "Environmentally  preferable  products"  means products that have a lesser or reduced effect
on human health and the environment  when compared  with competing  products serving the
same purpose, considering  raw materials  acquisition,  production,  manufacturing,  packaging,
distribution, use, reuse, operation,  maintenance,  and disposal.

B. "Recycled  product" means a product containing  post-consumer  waste, manufacturing scrap,
or other recovered  materials in amounts meeting or exceeding  the minimum content standards
adopted by the City Council or by administrative  policy.

C. "Practicable"  means sufficient  in performance  and available  at a reasonably  competitive  price
compared  to non-environmentally  preferable  alternatives,  considering  total cost of ownership
over the useful life of the product.

D. "Waste prevention"  means source  reduction  practices  that reduce  the volume  or toxicity  of
products consumed  or discarded.

Additional  definitions  may be adopted  by administrative  policy.

1.54.055  Standards  of Conduct;  Conflicts  of Interest;  Gratuities.

This Section  supplements,  and does not replace,  the conflict-of-interest  and ethics  requirements  imposed  by
Government  Code § 1090,  the Political  Reform  Act (Government  Code §§ 81000  et seq.), the regulations  of the
Fair Political  Practices  Commission,  the common  law conflict-of-interest  doctrine,  the City's conflict-of-interest
code adopted  under the Political  Reform  Act, and applicable  federal  requirements  includin@ 2 CFR § 200.318(c).

A. City elected  officials,  appointed  officials,  board  and commission  members,  officers,  employees,  and agents
involved  in the selection,  award,  or administration  of contracts (includin@ federally funded contracts subject to 2
CFR § 200.318(c))  shall avoid any real or apparent  conflicts  ofinterest.  No person  covered  by this subsection
shall participate  in the selection,  award,  or administration  of a contract  supported  by City or federal  funds  if a
real or apparent  conflict  ofinterest  would  be involved.  Such a conflict  arises when  an employee,  officer,  official,
or board  or commission  member,  or any member  of their  immediate  family,  has a financial  or other  interest  in,
or receives  a tangible  personal  benefit  from,  a firm considered  for a contract.  For purposes  of this Section,
"immediate family"  means spouse or rezistered domestic partner, parent, child, siblinH, parent-in-law, child-in-
law, or sibling-in-law,  whether  biolozical,  adoptive,  or by marriage.

B. City elected  officials,  appointed  officials,  board  and commission  members,  officers,  employees,  and agents
shall not solicit  or accept gratuities,  favors,  or anything  of monetary  value from  present  or prospective
contractors  or subcontractors  that could  reasonably  be perceived  to influence  a procurement  decision.

C. Violations  of this Section  are subject  to disciplinary  action  and may result  in remedies  up to and including
contract  termination,  disqualification,  or debarment  consistent  with  applicable  law.

D. Organizational  Conflicts  of Interest  (OCI). A person  or firm that  prepares  specifications,  statements  of work,  or
solicitation  documents  for a particular  procurement  shall not compete  for that  procurement,  unless the City
determines  in writing  that adequate  safeguards  have been implemented  to neutralize  or mitigate  the conflict
consistent  with applicable  law and fundinz-source  requirements.  The Administrative  Purchasing  Policies  and
Procedures  shall include  the standard  organizational  conflict-of-interest  guidelines  required  of local agencies
using desizn-build  or progressive  design-build delivery under Public Contract Code §§ 22160 et seq., 22170 et
seq., and 22185 et seq.

E. Debarment  and Suspension.  The City may debar  or suspend  a vendor,  contractor,  or consultant  for cause,
including,  but not limited  to, fraud,  collusion,  a criminal  offense  in connection  with obtaining  or performing  a
public  contract,  significant  or repeated  performance  failures,  or serious  ethical  violations.  The procedures,
notice,  and appeal  rights for debarment  or suspension  shall be established  by administrative  policy  consistent
with applicable  law.

  continue  monitoring  legislative  and regulatory  developments  related to the California  Values

  c.  Direct  the City  Maiiager  to ensure  that  all updated  model  policies  requited  by  SB 580

ANALYSIS:  The City  of South  Gate is committed  to upholding  the requirements  of the California
Values  Act  and maintaining  the trust  of all members  of the community.  The City  has implemented
comprehensive  measures to ensure full compliaxice  with the Act, as detailed  below:

Law Enforcement  Policies  and Practices

The South Gate Police  Department  does not use City resources  or personnel  to investigate,  interrogate,
detain,  detect,  or artest  persons  for  gration  enforcement  purposes,  consistent  w'th  Goyernment
Code section 7284,6(a)(I).  Officers  do not inquire  into individuals=  immigration  status for immigration
enforcement  purposes.

 The South  Gate Police  Department  has remained  steadfast  in its commitment  to adhering  to the
guidelines  set forth  by the California  Values  Act.  Department  policies  which  are in line with  California
Values  Act requirements  ensure that personnel  act in accordance  with  Senate Bill  54.

Since the inception  of Senate Bill  54, the South  Gate Police  Department  has not transferred  any people
in custody  to the custody  of ICE for violation  of civil  immigration  laws and does not honor  ICE
Detainer  requests.  The Police  Department  also complies  with  all annual  reporting  requirements  to the
California  Department  of Justice.

ICE  Detainer  and Transfer  Policies

The Police  Department  does not honor  ICE  hold  requests,  notification  requests,  or transfer  requests,
except  where  permitted  under  Government  Code  sections  7282.5  and 7284.6(a)(4)-specifically,  for
individuals  with  specified  serious  criminal  convictions  where  a judicial  warrant  has been obtained.

No Federal  Deputization  or Supervision

The City has not placed  any peace officers  under the supervision  of federal  agencies,  nor has it deputized
any  officers  as special  federal  officers  for  immigration  enforcement  purposes,  in accordance  with
Government  Code section  7284.6(a)(2).

No Dedicated  ICE  Space  or Detention  Contracts

The City  does not provide  office  space exclusively  dedicated  to immigration  authorities  or immigration
investigations  within  any  law  enforcement  facility,  as prohibited  by  Government  Code  section
7284.6(a)(5).  Furthermore,  the City does not have, and has not entered  into, any contracts  with the federal
government  to house  individuals  for civil  immigration  custody  purposes,  consistent  with  Governrnent
Code sections  7284.6(a)(6)  and 7310.

TRUTH  Act  Compliance

To the extent  applicable,  the City  complies  with  all TRUTH  Act  consent  and notification  requirements
set forth  in Government  Code  section  7283.1,  including  providing  written  consent  forms  prior  to ICE
interviews,  furnishing  copies  of ICE requests  to affected  individuals,  maintaining  public  records  of ICE
access, and holding  community  forums  as required.

Task  Force  Compliance

Any  participation  by South  Gate law enforcement  in joint  law enforcement  task forces  is limited  to task
forces  whose  primary  purpose  is not immigration  enforcement,  and whose  enforcement  or investigative
duties are primarily  related  to violations  of state or federal  law unrelated  to immigration  enforcement,  in
compliance  with  Government  Code section  7284.6(b)(3).

Reporting  Compliance

The City  has adopted  and implemented  model  policies  or equivalent  policies  as required  by Government

Training  and Community  Trust

City  staff  and  law  enforcement  officers  receive  training  on the  California  Values  Act  and related

regardless  of immigration  status, consistent  with the legislative  intent  of the Act to promote  trust between
immigrant  communities  and public  agencies.

BACKGROUND:  The California  Values  Act,  also la'iown  as Senate Bill  54 (SB 54), was signed  into
law on October  5, 2017, and took effect  on January  1, 2018. The Act is codified  at California  Government
Code  sections  7284  through  7284.12.  Its constitutionality  was upheld  by the Ninth  Circuit  Court  of
Appeals  in United  States v. California,  921 F.3d 865 (9th Cir. 2019).

The California  Values  Act  was enacted  to ensure that state and local  resources  are not used to assist in
federal  civil  immigration  enforcement,  thereby  preserving  the relationship  of trust between  California's
immigrant  cornrnunities  and state and local  government  agencies.  The Legislature  found  that this trust
is central  to the public  safety  of all Californians  and is threatened  when  state and local  agencies  become
entangled  with  federal  immigration  enforcement  operations.

Key legislative  findings  underlying  the Act include:

  *  ImmigrantsarevaluableandessentialmembersoftheCaliforniacommunity.A1mostoneinthree
  Californians  is foreign  born  and one in two  children  in California  has at least one immigrant
  parent.

  *  A relationship  of trust between  California's  immigrant  community  and state and local  agencies
  is central  to the public  safety  of all Californians.

  *  Entangling  state and local agencies  with  federal  immigration  enforcement  diverts  already  limited
  resources  and blurs the lines of accountability  between  local,  state, and federal  governtnents.

  *  State and local  participation  in federal  immigration  enforcement  raises  constitutional  concerns,
  including  possible  Fourth  Amendment  and Equal  Protection  violations.

 Additionally,  Senate Bill  580 (SB 580), effective  January  1, 2026, codified  at Government  Code section
12532.5,  requires  all state and local  agencies  to implement  the Attorney  General's  model  policies  or
equivalent  policies  by January  1, 2027, further  strengthening  the framework  established  by the California
Values  Act.

KEY  PROVISIONS

The  California  Values  Act  imposes  the following  requirements  and prohibitions  on California  law
enforcement  agencies:

Prohibitions  on Local  Law  Enforcement

Under  Governrnent  Code section  7284.6(a),  California  law enforcement  agencies  shall not:

  1.  Use agency  moneys  or personnel  to investigate,  interrogate,  detain,  detect,  or arrest persons  for
  immigration  enforcement  purposes,  including  inquiring  into an individual's  immigration  status.

  2.  Honor  ICE  hold  requests,  notification  requests,  or  transfer  requests,  except  in  limited
  circumstances  involving  individuals  with  specified  serious  criminal  convictions  and judicial
  warrants.

  3.  Provide  personal  information  about  an  individual,  such  as home  or  work  addresses,  to
  immigration  authorities  unless  such information  is publicly  available.

  4.  Make  or intentionally  participate  in arrests based on civil  immigration  warrants.

  5.  Place  peace  officers  under  the supervision  of federal  agencies  or deputize  officers  as special
  federal  officers  for immigration  enforcement  purposes.

  6.  Use irnrnigration  authorities  as interpreters  for law enforcement  matters.

  7.  Transferindividualstoimtnigrationauthoritiesunlessauthorizedbyajudicialwarrantorjudicial
  probable  cause determination.

  8.  Provide  office  space exclusively  dedicated  to immigration  authorities  within  law enforcement
  facilities.

  9.  Contract  with  the federal  government  to use law enforcement  facilities  to house individuals  for
  civil  immigration  custody.

Permitted  Activities

The Act does not prevent  California  law enforcement  from:

  *  Investigating  or arresting  individuals  for violation  of 8 U.S.C.  § 1326(a)  (illegal  reentry  subject
  to felony  enhancement)  when detected  during  unrelated  law enforcement  activity.

  Enforcement  Telecommunications  System  (CLETS).

  *  Conducting  enforcement  or investigative  duties  associated  with  joint  law  enforcement  task
  forces,  provided  the primary  purpose  of the task force  is not irnrnigration  enforcement.

  *  Making  inquiries  to certify  T or U Visa victims.

  *  Giving  immigration  authorities  access to interview  an individual  in custody,  subject  to TRUTH

TRUTH  Act  Requirements

Under  Government  Code section  7283. 1, the TRUTH  Act requires  local  law enforcement  agencies  to:

  *  Provide  a written  consent  fornn before  any interview  between  ICE  and an individual  in local
  custody  regarding  civil  immigration  violations,  explaining  that the interview  is voluntary.

  *  Provide  a copy  of any ICE  hold,  notification,  or transfer  request  to the affected  individual  and
  inform  the individual  whether  the agency  intends  to comply.

  *  Maintain  all records  relating  to ICE access as public  records.

  *  Hold  at least one annual  community  forum  if ICE access was provided  during  the prior  year.

Reporting  and Model  Policies

Law enforcement  agencies  must submit  annual  reports  to the California  Department  of Justice  regarding
any joint  task force participation  and any transfers  to immigration  authorities.  The Attorney  General  has
issued updated  model  policies  for schools,  libraries,  healthcare  facilities,  courthouses,  shelters,  and labor
agencies,  most recently  in December  2024 and July 2026 pursuant  to SB 580.

Design  Review  is an administrative  (staff  level)  process  that does not require  a public  hearing.

Pursuant  to SGMC  Section  11.22.060,  the purpose  of the IF zone is to continue  the industrial  job  base in
the area, while  allowing  flexibility  to incorporate  a mix  of uses and job  options,  supporting  innovative
industry  and living  options  in close proximity  to transit,  existing  employment  centers,  and major  corridors.
Furthermore,  pursuant  to SGMC  Section  11.24.060,  light  and heavy  manufacturing  (M2  and M3)  zones are
intended  to implement  the manufacturing/distribution  place  type  designation  of the General  Plan.  These
zones  include  uses such  as industrial,  manufacturing,  large-scale  warehouse,  distribution,  or logistics
facilities.  The M3 zone provides  dedicated  locations  for the preservation  and development  of commercial
and industrial  activities.

Properties  along Rayo Avenue,  between  Firestone  Boulevard  and Southern  Avenue,  are currently  designated
M3 and predominantly  occupied  by industrial  uses, with  the exception  of the LAUSD  facility  to the south
of the project  site at 5115  Southern  Avenue,  which  is designated  IF. The front  portion  of the subject  site,
which  abuts Rayo  Avenue,  is also designated  M3,  aligning  with  the zoning  of most  properties  along  the
street. Therefore,  maintaining  this M3  zoning  designation  is appropriate  to ensure  continued  compatibility
with  existing  and future  industrial  uses on adjacent  properties.  The rear portion  of the site is designated  IF
and shares  boundaries  with  other  IF-designated  parcels  that  front  Atlantic  Avenue.  The  proposed  zone
change  for the rear portion  of the site supports  this zoning  pattern  and reinforces  consistency  along  Atlantic
Avenue.  Furthermore,  the change  would  facilitate  future  development  that aligns  with  surrounding  uses.

Environmental  Review
The proposed  Zone Change  constitutes  a "project"  under the California  Environmental  QualityAct  (CEQA).
The City  of South Gate is the LeadAgency,  and an Initial  Study  (IS) was prepared  by EcoTierra  Consulting,
Inc. in July 2026 to determine  whether  the Zone  Change  and the related  site improvements  could  result  in
significant  effects  on the environment.  The Initial  Study  evaluated  all twenty  CEQA  environmental  topic
areas,  including  aesthetics,  air  quality,  biological  and  cultural  resources,  energy,  geology  and  soils,
greenhouse  gas emissions,  hazards  and hazardous  materials,  hydrology  and water  quality,  land  use and
planning,  noise, public  services,  transportation,  tribal  cultural  resources,  utilities,  and wildfire.

The analysis  considered  not only the map amendment  itself  but also the physical  improvements  the applicant
proposes  if the Zone  Change  is approved  -  paving  and striping  of a new vehicle  storage  area, new  site
lighting,  and construction  of an approximately  560-square-foot  office  building  -  along with  approximately
52 cubic yards of soil cut, all of which  would  be exported,  and roughly  eight months  of construction  actiyity
begiru"iing  in the first  quarter  of 2027.

Basis for Environmental  Concern.
As described  in the Background  section  above,  the site was used for drum  recycling  and reconditioning
operations  from  the 1940s  until  2003  and has been listed  by the United  States Environmental  Protection
Agency  (EPA)  on the  Superfund  National  Priorities  List.  Known  soil  and  groundwater  contamination
remains,  and EPA continues  to oversee  cleanup  activities  at the site. The Initial  Study  therefore  focused  on
whether  ground-disturbing  activities  associated  with the proposed  site improvements  could  expose  workers,
the public,  or the environment  to hazardous  materials,  or degrade  water  quality.

Findings.
The Initial  Study  determined  that the project  would  result  in no impact  or a less-than-significant  impact  in
all environmental  topic  areas except  Hazards  and Hazardous  Materials  and Hydrology  and Water  Quality,
which  were found  to be potentially  significant  unless mitigated.  Because  these two areas could  be reduced
to a less-than-significant  level  through  mitigation,  the corresponding  Mandatory  Findings  of Significance
were likewise  identified  as potentially  significant  unless mitigated.  No mitigation  was required  in any other
topic  area.

Mitigation  Measure.
One mitigation  measure  was identified,  which  addresses  both areas of potential  impact:

  *  MM-HAZ-1:  Prior  to commencement  of any on-site  grading,  a Focused  Soil  Management  Plan
  ("SMP")  shall  be approved  in  accordance  with  the  requirements  of the  Department  of Toxic
  Substances  Control  (DTSC),  U.S.  EPA,  the  South  Coast  Air  Quality  Management  District
  (SCAQMD),  and the Los Angeles  Regional  Water  Quality  Control  Board  (LARWQCB).  The SMP
  shall establish  procedures  for managing  soil disturbance  activities  associated  with  the proposed  site
  improvements  based  on existing  soil  data,  and shall  define  protocols  for  addressing  previously
  unknown  soil impacts  encountered  during  construction.  The SMP shall provide  guidance  for work
  in  areas  of known  contamination  and  outline  contingency  measures  if previously  unidentified
  hazardous  materials  or subsurface  features  (such as underground  storage  tanks,  sumps,  clarifiers,  or
  septic tanks)  are encountered.  The SMP shall also address  soil management,  movement,  temporary
  storage,  and disposal  associated  with  site improvement  activities.

Conclusion  of Enyironmental  Review.
With  incorporation  of  MM-HAZ-1,  all  potentially  significant  impacts  would  be reduced  to less-than-
significant  levels.  Accordingly,  a Mitigated  Negative  Declaration  (MND)  was prepared  rather  than  an
Environmental  Impact  Report,  consistent  with  Section  15070  of the State CEQA  Guidelines.  The IS/MND
was circulated  for a public  review  and cornrnent  period  beginning  July  24, 2026,  and ending  August  24,
2026,  and notice  was published  online  and in the South  Gate Press.  Prior  to taking  action  on the Zone
Change,  the City  Council  must first  consider  and adopt the IS/MND.

CONCLUSION:

Based on the above analysis, staff has determined the proposed Zone Change will maintain consistency  with
the General Plan. The amendment supports the community's  long-term vision by promoting  orderly
development,  aligning  land use designations with current needs, and ensuring  compatibility  with
surrounding uses. Therefore, staff recommends approval of the Zone Change request.

Expanding  the existing  contract  will  allow  the work  to proceed  without  the time  and expense  of
selecting  and bringing  a new consultant  up to speed.

Amendment  No. 1 will  add to the services  described  in Exhibit  A and increase  the contract  by an

reimbursement  under the CalRecycle  SB1383  Local  Assistance  Grant.  Go2Zero  will  be paid only
for eligible  work,  completed  and properly  invoiced.  No General  Fund  money  will  be used. Any
grant funds not used by the November  2026 deadline  must be returned  to CalRecycle.

$282,330.  All  other terms and conditions  of the existing  contract  will  remain  unchanged.  Approval
of Amendment  No. 1 will  allow  the City  to complete  the grant-'[unded  work  on time  and continue
meeting  its SB 1383 requirements.

BACKGROUND:  Senate Bill  (SB) 1383,  enacted  in 2016,  established  statewide  requirements  to
reduce  organic  waste  sent to landfills  and increase  the recovery  of edible  food.  The regulations
implementing  SB 1383 took effect  on January  1, 2022.

To help local  agencies  comply  with  these requirements,  CalRecycle  provided  the city  with  one-
time grant funding  for approved  activities.  The city received  the funding  in two allocations  totaling
$247,931.

On  January  14,  2025,  the  City  Council  approved  Contract  No.  2025-04-CC  with  Go2Zero
Strategies,  LLC,  for  an amount  not  to exceed  $282,330  over  a three-year  term.  The  contract
provides  specialized  solid waste management  services,  including  regulatory  compliance,  program
management,  edible  food  recovery,  public  outreach,  capacity  planning,  and  required
recordkeeping  and reporting.

As the City  implemented  its SB 1383 programs,  staff identified  additional  grant-eligible  work  that
was not included  in the original  contract.  Amendment  No.  l adds compliance  assistance,  public
education  and outreach,  edible  food  recovery  support,  equipment  distribution,  a recordkeeping
system,  and grant administration  support.  These services  will  build  upon Go2Zero's  existing  work
and help the City  complete  the approved  grant activities  within  the required  timeframe.

  SUBJECT: RATIFICATJON OF AN ACRF,EMT.Yt' WtTH ALL CITY MANAGEMENT
  SERVICES, INC., FOR CROSSING GUARD SERVICES, AND APPROVAL  OF A
  RELATED BUDGE,T AMENDMENT

  PURPOSE:  ToratifyanagreementwithAllCityManagementServices,Inc.,forCrossingGuard
  Services at 17 school crossing locations, and to appropriate funds for the agreement, The service
  provides for the safety of students, parents, and staff walking to and from school by staffing
  designated intersections during peak periods of pedestrian activity.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTION: The City Council will considet:
  a. Ratifying an Agreement with All City Management Services, Inc, ("ACMS"), for crossing
  guard services for a term of August 31, 2026, through December 18, 2026, in an amount
  not to exceed $153,400; and
  b. Approvingabudgetamendmentappropriating$153,400fromtheGeneralFundBudget
  Stabilization Reserve to account 100-505-21-6109 in the Fiscal Year 2026-2027 budget.

  FISCAL IMPACT: The not-to-exceed cost of the agreement is $I53,400, That figure reflects 17
  crossing locations staffed approximately three hours per day across approximately 76 instructional
  days, for a total of 3,864 service hours at the contract rate of $39.70 per hour,

  ACMS increased its hourly rate from $34,80 in Fiscal Year 2025-2026 to $39.70 in Fiscal Year
  2026-2027, an increase of 14,lpercent. ACMS attributes the increase to rising wages and operating
  costs.

  Funds for crossing guard services were not included in the FY2026-2027 budget because the
  program was eliminated as part of citywide budget reductions, Approval of this item therefore
  requires a new appropriation. Staff recommend funding the appropriatiori from the General Fund
  Budget  Stabilization  Reserve.

  The Budget Stabilization Reserve balance is currently $1,518,527. Appropriating $153,400 would
  reduce the balance to $1,365,127, a reduction of 10.1 percent of the Budget Stabilization Reserve.

  172
 The City  Council  should  be aware of the trade-off  this action  presents.  Crossing  guard  service  is a
recurring  operating  cost, and reserves  are one-time  money.  Using  reserves  to fund recurring  costs
reduces  the City's  capacity  to absorb  future  revenue  shortfalls  or emergencies,  and it does not
resolve  the underlying  structural  gap that led to the program's  elimination.  Staff  is presenting  this
option  because  the Council  has directed  the restoration  of service.

For context,  the prior  program  covered  37 locations  at an annual  cost of approximately  $750,000.
Continuing  the reduced  1 7-location  program  through  a 'full school  year is not currently  budgeted
for the spring  semester.

BACKGROUND:  Since  August  of 1994,  the City  has contracted  with  All  City  Management
Services,  Inc., to provide  crossing  guard services  throughout  the City.  The decision  to contract  this
operation  was based on cost savings  and increased  operational  services.  Before  the contract,  the
Police  Department  was responsible  for staffing  crossing  locations  when  a crossing  guard  could  not
fill  a shift,  and a sworn  officer  was often  pulled  from  patrol  to provide  coverage.  Contracting  the
service  transfers  that staffing  responsibility  to the vendor.  The Police  Department  has been satisfied
with  the services  ACMS  provides.

The crossing  guard  program  was eliminated  effective  July  1, 2026,  as part  of citywide  budget
reductions,  and the  ACMS  agreement  was  not  renewed  for  the  2026-2027  school  year.  Staff
approached  the school  district  regarding  shared  funding  of the program.  The district  declined  to
contribute.

The agreement  term runs from August  31, 2026, the first day of the school  year, through  December
18, 2026, the start of the winter  break.

At its meeting  on August  25, 2026,  the City  Council  directed  the City  Manager  to move  forward
expeditiously  in executing  an agreement  with  ACMS  so crossing  guards  could be deployed  as soon
as possible  for student  safety.  The Council  specifically  asked that the executed  agreement  return
for ratification  and directed  that execution  not be delayed  until  the September  8, 2026,  meeting
because  doing  so would  postpone  deployment  past the start of the school  year.

Consistent  with  that direction,  the agreement  was executed  on August  31, 2026, with  the signature
of the Mayor.  The City  Attorney  has approved  the agreement  as to form.  Crossing  guard  services
began on August  31, 2026,  and are currently  being  provided.  Ratification  confirms  and adopts  the
execution  of the agreement  retroactive  to the  start  of the term,  and the accompanying  budget
amendment  provides  the appropriation  necessary  to pay for the services.

ANALYSIS:  The proposed  Agreement  was procured  through  a competitive  bidding  process.  On
August  27, 2026,  the City  Clerk  received  and publicly  opened  three bids,  with  AAA  submitting
the lowest  bid. The bid documents  required  contractors  to submit  a "Revised  Base Bid No. 1" for
the proposed  street  improvements  and  an "Alternate  Bid"  for  the  construction  of pickleball
courts.  The bid  documents  further  specified  that the lowest  bidder  would  be determined  based
solely  on Revised  Base Bid No. 1. Accordingly,  AAA  was determined  to be the lowest  bidder.

AAA's  original  bid was $2,280,934.  During  staff's  routine  bid verification,  mathematical  errors
were  identified  in  AAA's  bid  calculations.  In  accordance  with  the  bid  requirements,  staff
corrected  the bid using  AAA's  submitted  unit  prices,  resulting  in a revised  "Revised  Base Bid
No.  1"  amount  of  $2,233,666.  The  revised  bid was lower  than  the  original  bid, thus,  the
correction  did  not  affect  the  bid  ranking,  and  AAA  remained  the  lowest  responsive  and
responsible  bidder.

The Project was budgeted based on the Engineer's Estimate of $3.46 million, prepared prior to
bidding. When bids were opened, the lowest bid came in significantly under budget, resulting in
more than $1.1 million in available Project funding.  Given the favorable unit prices received
through the competitive bidding process, it is financially  advantageous to use the available
Project funding to complete additional street improvements at the same competitive prices. This
allows the City to rehabilitate more streets with funding already budgeted for the Project,
maximizes the value of the existing construction contract, and avoids the additional costs and
delays associated with advertising and awarding a separate future project. Accordingly,  staff is
recommending that the City Council approve Contract Change Order No. 1 in an amount not-to-
exceed $1,500,000. The additional 'Junding would be used to rehabilitate  and slurry seal
additional streets throughout the City. The specific streets and project limits are currently being
identified by the Public Works Department; however, it is anticipated that approximately  13
additional streets will receive improvements.  The streets are identified in Attachment "A." The
final list of streets to be improved will be based on actual construction costs and may therefore
be expanded or reduced accordingly.

Appropriating  $960,000 in Community  Development  Block Grant

Community  Development Block Grant ("CDBG")  funds recently became available to the City
and must be fully expended by December 15, 2026. The City has programmed $960,000 of these
funds for use on Phase V of the Residential Resurfacing Project. The CDBG fiinds will be used
to construct street improvements  on Elizabeth Avenue, Virginia Avenue, Madison Avenue,
Cypress  Avenue,  South Gate Avenue, and Minnesota Avenue, as well as to convert an existing
tennis-court  area at South Gate Park into eight pickleball courts. These improvements  have been
incorporated into the Project scope. Accordingly,  staff is requesting that the City Council
appropriate $960,000 in CDBG funds to the Project  so the funds  can be used for  these
improvements within the required expendihire deadline.

Construction  Contingency  and City Manager  Change Order  Authority

Finally,  staffrecommends that the City Council authorize the City Manager to approve contract
change orders within the $250,000 construction  contingency, exclusive of Contract Change
Order No. 1. This authority will allow necessary field changes, quantity adjustments, and other
unforeseen  work to be addressed promptly  during the 80-working-day  construction period
without  delaying the Project. All approved change orders will be reported to the City Council at
Project closeout.

 ANALYSIS:  The Water  Main  Replacement  Project  will  replace  approximately  8,000  linear  feet
of  aging  water  mains  and  install  Advanced  Meter  Reading  water  meters  and  related
improvements  on the West side of the City.

The City  advertised  the project  for construction  bids on June 17, 2026,  and received  seven bids
on July 20, 2026,  listed  here.

  Bidder  Name  Bid
  O'Duffy  $4,454,711
  Williams  Pipeline  $4,697,722
  JA Salazar  $5,021,546
  Stephen  Doreck  $5,307,481
  Gentry  General  $5,934,232
  Big Ben  $6,224,836
  Dominguez  General  $6,523,168

O'Duffy  Bros.,  Inc. submitted  the lowest  bid at $4,454,711.  Following  the bid opening,  the City
received  a written  protest  from  Williams  Pipeline  Contractors,  Inc.,  challenging  O'Duffy's  bid
based on an omitted  signature  on one page of the bid documents.  Furthermore,  during  its review
of  the  bid,  staff  also  identified  an arithmetic  discrepancy:  O'Duffy's  bid  listed  a total  of
$4,454,711,  while  the  total  calculated  from  the  submitted  unit  prices  and  quantities  was
$4,454,728.

In consultation  with  the City  Attorney's  Office,  staff  deternnined  that both the omitted  signature
and the arithmetic  discrepancy  constituted  minor,  waivable  irregularities.  The bid was otherwise
complete,  was signed  in all other required  locations,  included  a valid  bid bond,  and demonstrated
O'Duffy's  intent  to be bound  by its terms.  Neither  irregularity  compromised  the competitive
bidding  process  or provided  O'Duf'fy  with  a competitive  advantage,  and  correction  of  the
arithmetic  discrepancy  did not alter O'Duffy's  status as the lowest  bidder.  Accordingly,  the City
denied  the  bid  protest  and  determined  that  O'Duffy  remains  the  lowest  responsive  and
responsible  bidder.  Staff  therefore  recommend  awarding  the construction  agreement  to O'Duffy
in an amount  not to exceed  $4,454,728.

Staff  recommend  authorizing  the City  Manager  to approve  and execute  change  orders  up to a
cumulative  amount  of $601,000  within  the approved  project  budget.  Construction  projects  of this
nature  may encounter  unforeseen  subsurface  conditions,  utility  conflicts,  quantity  adjustments,  or
other necessary  field  changes.  This authority  will  allow  the City  to address  such issues promptly,
minimize  construction  delays  and  associated  costs,  and  maintain  the  project  schedule  while
ensuring  that all change  orders remain  within  the approved  budget.

BACKGROUND:  The  City's  water  distribution  system  includes  water  mains  that  have
reached  the end of their  use:tul  service  life  and require  replacement  to maintain  the system's
reliability  and integrity.  The City  developed  the Water  Main  Replacement  Project  to address  this
aging  infrastructure  through  a phased program  of improvements.

The current  project  will  enhance  the City's  water  infrastructure  on the West  side of the City  by
replacing  approximately  8,000 linear  feet of aging  water mains  at the following  locations:

  2

  226
   State Street, between  Tweedy  Boulevard  and Southern  Avenue

  Sequoia  Drive,  between  State Street and Elizabeth  Avenue

  Michigan  Avenue,  between  Elizabeth  Avenue  and California  Avenue

  *  Elizabeth  Avenue,  between  Michigan  Avenue  and Martin  Luther  King  Jr. Drive

  *  Dolores  Avenue,  between  Seminole  Avenue  and Martin  Luther  King  Jr. Drive

  *  Meadows  Avenue

In addition  to replacing  the water  mains,  the project  includes  installing  Advanced  Meter  Reading
water  meters,  valves,  fittings,  service  laterals,  fire  hydrants,  and  other  related  water-system
improvements.  These improvements  are intended  to reduce  the potential  for water-main  failures,
improve  system  reliability,  and  support  the continued  delivery  of safe and dependable  water
service  to residents  and businesses.

Pursuant  to the guidelines  of the California  Environmental  Quality  Act  (CEQA),  this project  is
categorically  exempt  under  Title  14 of the California  Code of Regulations,  Section  15301,  Class
I(c)  exemption  for replacement  of existing  utility  infrastructure

Construction  is anticipated  to begin  in November  2026 and be completed  by February  2027.
